species.where: Hard, flat shelves on dead and dying hardwoods; lasts for years.
features: Woody, flat shelf up to 50 cm, gray-brown top often dusted with brown spores
White pore surface that turns dark brown when scratched
New layer each year
species.lookalikes: Hemlock varnish shelf has a shiny red top. Red-belted conk (Fomitopsis) has a red band near the edge.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.search: artist's conk ganoderma applanatum hard, flat shelves on dead and dying hardwoods; lasts for years.

species.where: Only on dead or dying birch.
features: Smooth, rounded, pale tan to white bracket with a rolled edge
White pores underneath
Soft, corky flesh
species.lookalikes: Few look-alikes on birch. Tinder polypore (Fomes) on birch is hoof-shaped and hard.
species.search: birch polypore fomitopsis betulina only on dead or dying birch.

species.where: On soil or well-rotted wood under hemlock and hardwoods.
features: Tan to brown cap
Pores white then pinkish
Coarse dark-brown net on the stem
Very bitter taste
species.lookalikes: King bolete has white to olive pores and a pale net.

photo.author:
Tylopilus_felleus_060914c.jpg: bernd gliwa
derivative work: Ak ccm

species.search: bitter bolete tylopilus felleus on soil or well-rotted wood under hemlock and hardwoods.

species.where: In moss and leaf litter under oak and beech, often on slopes.
features: Gray-black, hollow, trumpet-shaped
Smooth to slightly wrinkled outer surface, no gills
Hard to see against dark leaves
species.lookalikes: Few look-alikes. Black earth tongues and some cup fungi are dark but not hollow trumpets.
species.note: California has a winter relative, C. calicornucopioides.
species.search: black trumpet craterellus fallax in moss and leaf litter under oak and beech, often on slopes.

species.where: On soil under conifers.
features: Whitish, lumpy cap that 'bleeds' bright red drops when young
Short teeth underneath instead of gills
Tough, corky flesh
species.lookalikes: Other Hydnellum species lack the red droplets. Not dangerous, but inedible.
species.search: bleeding tooth hydnellum peckii on soil under conifers.

species.where: On living birch trunks in northern forests.
features: Black, deeply cracked, charcoal-like lump on the trunk
Rusty orange-brown inside
Not a cap or shelf; it is a sterile mass
species.lookalikes: Burls and black knots on trees look similar; chaga is orange inside.
species.search: chaga inonotus obliquus on living birch trunks in northern forests.

species.where: Singly or scattered on soil under oak, beech, and other hardwoods in the East; under Douglas-fir and other conifers in the West.
features: Egg-yolk yellow to orange
Blunt, forking ridges (false gills) that run down the stem
Solid white flesh, often a fruity smell
species.lookalikes: Jack-o'-lantern has sharp true gills and grows in clusters on wood. False chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca) has thin, true forked gills.
species.note: Eastern fruiting is summer; Pacific Northwest is fall; California is winter. Several species are recognized.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.season_label: Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec
species.search: chanterelle cantharellus species singly or scattered on soil under oak, beech, and other hardwoods in the east; under douglas-fir and other conifers in the west.

species.where: Overlapping shelves on living or dead hardwoods, especially oak.
features: Bright orange shelves with sulfur-yellow edges
Yellow pore surface underneath, no gills
Soft and moist when young, chalky when old
species.lookalikes: Jack-o'-lantern is orange but has gills. Western species on conifers and eucalyptus (L. conifericola, L. gilbertsonii) are more often linked to bad reactions.
species.search: chicken of the woods laetiporus sulphureus overlapping shelves on living or dead hardwoods, especially oak.

species.where: Clusters in grass, often over buried wood or roots.
features: Gray-brown, bell-shaped cap, smooth or faintly scaly
Gills turn black and dissolve into ink
Grows in tight clusters
species.lookalikes: Shaggy mane is white and shaggy and grows singly or scattered.
species.note: Contains coprine, which causes nausea and flushing if alcohol is taken within a few days.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.season_label: Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct
species.search: common ink cap coprinopsis atramentaria clusters in grass, often over buried wood or roots.

species.where: On rotting wood, especially conifer logs, often among moss.
features: Small brown cap 1 to 4 cm, drying lighter
Brown gills; rusty brown spore print
Thin ring on the stem that often fades to a band
species.lookalikes: Honey mushroom, velvet foot, and other small brown mushrooms on wood. Its toxins are the same type as the death cap's.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.season_label: Apr, May, Jun, Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec
species.search: deadly galerina galerina marginata on rotting wood, especially conifer logs, often among moss.

species.where: On soil under oaks and introduced trees; common in coastal California and spreading in the Pacific Northwest. Rare and local in the Northeast.
features: Greenish, yellowish, or bronze cap
White gills and white spore print
Ring on the stem and a sac-like cup at the base
species.lookalikes: Mistaken for paddy straw and other edible mushrooms, especially by people who learned mushrooms elsewhere.
species.note: Causes most fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide.
species.season_label: Jan, Feb, Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec
species.search: death cap amanita phalloides on soil under oaks and introduced trees; common in coastal california and spreading in the pacific northwest. rare and local in the northeast.

species.where: On soil in woods and at wood edges, sometimes in lawns near trees.
features: All white, smooth cap
White gills free from the stem; white spore print
Skirt-like ring on the stem
Sac-like cup (volva) at the base, often buried; dig it up to see it
species.lookalikes: White Agaricus (meadow and horse mushrooms) have pink to dark brown gills and no cup. Buttons can look like puffballs.
species.note: One cap can kill. In California A. ocreata fruits in late winter and spring.
species.search: destroying angel amanita bisporigera (east), a. ocreata (california) on soil in woods and at wood edges, sometimes in lawns near trees.

species.where: On dead or dying elm, maple, and other hardwoods.
features: Large cream cap with brown feather-like scales
Big angular pores underneath
Smells like watermelon rind
species.lookalikes: No dangerous look-alikes.
species.note: Most common in spring, around morel season.
species.search: dryad's saddle (pheasant back) cerioporus squamosus on dead or dying elm, maple, and other hardwoods.

species.where: In rings or arcs in lawns and pastures, often with a ring of darker grass.
features: Tan cap 1 to 5 cm with a low central bump
Widely spaced gills
Tough, wiry stem that bends without snapping
Dries out and revives after rain
species.lookalikes: Sweating mushrooms (Clitocybe dealbata and relatives) also grow in lawn rings, are whitish with crowded gills, and contain muscarine.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.season_label: May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct
species.search: fairy ring mushroom marasmius oreades in rings or arcs in lawns and pastures, often with a ring of darker grass.

species.where: On soil under conifers, especially pine and aspen-pine woods, in spring.
features: Reddish-brown, brain-like or wrinkled cap, not pitted
Cut lengthwise, the inside is chambered or cottony, not one hollow
Cap lobes fused to the stem in places
species.lookalikes: True morels are fully hollow with a pitted cap.
species.note: Contains gyromitrin, which can be deadly.
species.search: false morel gyromitra esculenta on soil under conifers, especially pine and aspen-pine woods, in spring.

species.where: On soil under conifers and birch, often in rings.
features: Cap red (West) or yellow to orange (much of the East) with white warty patches
White gills and stem
A ring and a swollen base with rings of scales
species.lookalikes: Other Amanitas, including deadly ones, share the ring and swollen base. Do not use cap color alone.
species.note: North American forms are often split as varieties or separate species.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.search: fly agaric amanita muscaria on soil under conifers and birch, often in rings.

species.where: On soil and leaf litter in woods, along trails, and sometimes in grass.
features: Pear-shaped, white to tan, 2 to 6 cm
Covered in small cone-shaped spines that rub off and leave a net pattern
Opens at a hole on top and puffs brown spores
species.lookalikes: Young Amanita buttons look like small puffballs; cut them in half and look for a mushroom outline. Pigskin poison puffball is firm and dark purple-black inside.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.search: gem-studded puffball lycoperdon perlatum on soil and leaf litter in woods, along trails, and sometimes in grass.

species.where: Lawns, pastures, field edges, and open woods.
features: White ball the size of a soccer ball or bigger
No stem, cap, or gills
Solid pure white inside when young, olive-brown powder when old
species.lookalikes: Smaller white 'puffballs' can be Amanita buttons. Cut every one top to bottom: an outline of a cap, gills, or stem inside means Amanita, which can be deadly. Earthballs are firm and dark inside.

photo.author: The original uploader was Sulfur at English Wikipedia.

species.search: giant puffball calvatia gigantea lawns, pastures, field edges, and open woods.

species.where: Lawns and parks, often in large rings or arcs.
features: Large white cap with brownish scales, 10 to 30 cm
Gills white, turning gray-green with age; green spore print
Movable ring on the stem
species.lookalikes: Parasols and shaggy parasols (Macrolepiota, Chlorophyllum rhacodes) have white spore prints. A spore print is the only reliable way to separate them.
species.note: The most often reported cause of mushroom poisoning in North America. More common in warmer regions.
species.search: green-spored parasol chlorophyllum molybdites lawns and parks, often in large rings or arcs.

species.where: On dead or dying eastern hemlock, sometimes other conifers.
features: Shiny, lacquered red to red-brown top
White to cream pores underneath
Often has a short side stem
species.lookalikes: Lacquered polypores on hardwoods are related (G. sessile and others). None are deadly.
species.note: Fresh growth in summer; old shelves stay visible longer.
species.season_label: May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct
species.search: hemlock varnish shelf ganoderma tsugae on dead or dying eastern hemlock, sometimes other conifers.

species.where: A large rosette at the base of oaks, usually living ones, often in the same spot each year.
features: Many gray-brown, spoon-shaped caps from a branched base
White pores underneath
Clusters up to 50 cm across
species.lookalikes: Black-staining polypore (Meripilus sumstinei) has larger caps that bruise black. Berkeley's polypore (Bondarzewia berkeleyi) is cream with fewer, much larger caps.
species.search: hen of the woods (maitake) grifola frondosa a large rosette at the base of oaks, usually living ones, often in the same spot each year.

species.where: Dense clusters at the base of living or dead trees and stumps, or from buried roots.
features: Honey-yellow to brown caps with small dark hairs near the center
White to cream gills; white spore print
A ring on the stem in A. mellea
Black, bootlace-like strands (rhizomorphs) under bark
species.lookalikes: Deadly galerina (Galerina marginata) grows on wood too and has a rusty brown spore print. Jack-o'-lantern is orange with no ring. Sulfur tuft has greenish-yellow gills and a dark spore print.
species.note: Armillaria is a group of similar species; experts split it further.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.search: honey mushroom armillaria mellea group dense clusters at the base of living or dead trees and stumps, or from buried roots.

species.where: Clusters at the base of hardwood stumps, especially oak, or from buried roots.
features: Bright orange caps and stems in tight clusters
True, sharp-edged gills that run down the stem
Orange flesh throughout
Gills can glow faintly in the dark
species.lookalikes: Chanterelles grow singly from soil and have blunt, forking false ridges, not sharp gills. Chicken of the woods has no gills.
species.note: Causes severe vomiting and cramps. In California a related species, O. olivascens, is olive-orange.
species.search: jack-o'-lantern omphalotus illudens clusters at the base of hardwood stumps, especially oak, or from buried roots.

species.where: On soil under spruce, pine, fir, and hemlock; in places also birch and oak.
features: Brown, bun-shaped cap
Pores white when young, aging yellow to olive; flesh does not turn blue
Thick stem with a fine white net near the top
species.lookalikes: Bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus) has pinkish pores and a dark net on the stem. Some red-pored boletes that bruise blue are toxic.
species.note: Western populations are often split into separate species.
species.search: king bolete boletus edulis group on soil under spruce, pine, fir, and hemlock; in places also birch and oak.

species.where: On wounds of living hardwoods or dead logs, especially oak, beech, and maple.
features: A white clump of long hanging spines, no cap
Spines 1 to 4 cm
Yellows with age
species.lookalikes: Other Hericium species (comb tooth, bear's head) are branched with shorter spines. None are known to be dangerous.

photo.author: (c) Alison Northup, some rights reserved (CC BY)

species.search: lion's mane hericium erinaceus on wounds of living hardwoods or dead logs, especially oak, beech, and maple.

species.where: On soil in mixed woods; it is a mold that covers certain Russula and Lactifluus mushrooms.
features: Bright orange-red, bumpy skin
Twisted, gill-less shape of the host underneath
White, firm flesh
species.lookalikes: Few look-alikes. The mold hides the host mushroom, so the host itself cannot be identified.
species.search: lobster mushroom hypomyces lactifluorum on soil in mixed woods; it is a mold that covers certain russula and lactifluus mushrooms.

species.where: Lawns, pastures, and grassy fields, often after rain.
features: White cap 3 to 10 cm
Gills pink when young, chocolate-brown when old; dark brown spore print
Thin ring; no cup at the base
species.lookalikes: Destroying angels have white gills and a cup. Yellow stainer (Agaricus xanthodermus) turns bright yellow at the stem base and smells of ink or phenol.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.search: meadow mushroom agaricus campestris lawns, pastures, and grassy fields, often after rain.

species.where: On soil near dying elms, ash, old apple orchards, and tulip poplar; in the West, also on burns.
features: Honeycomb cap with pits and ridges
Cap attached directly to the stem
Completely hollow from cap tip to stem base when cut lengthwise
species.lookalikes: False morels (Gyromitra) are brain-like and stuffed with cottony chambers. Early false morel (Verpa bohemica) has a cap that hangs free like a thimble.
species.note: Spring only. Timing follows warming soil, moving north and up in elevation.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.search: morel morchella species on soil near dying elms, ash, old apple orchards, and tulip poplar; in the west, also on burns.

species.where: On soil under oaks and other hardwoods.
features: Cap covered in shaggy gray-black scales
Gray pores that bruise red then black
Shaggy stem
species.lookalikes: No dangerous look-alikes; the black-and-white shaggy look is distinctive.

photo.author: This image was created by user Patrick Harvey (pg_harvey) at Mushroom Observer, a source for mycological images.You can contact this user here.

species.search: old man of the woods strobilomyces strobilaceus group on soil under oaks and other hardwoods.

species.where: Overlapping shelves on dead or dying hardwoods.
features: Fan-shaped white to gray-brown caps
Gills run down to a short, off-center stem or none
White to lilac spore print
species.lookalikes: Angel wings (Pleurocybella porrigens) are thin, all white, and on conifer wood; they have been linked to deaths. Mock oyster (Phyllotopsis nidulans) is orange and smells bad.
species.note: P. ostreatus favors cool weather. The look-alike P. pulmonarius fruits in summer.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.season_label: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, May, Oct, Nov, Dec
species.search: oyster mushroom pleurotus ostreatus group overlapping shelves on dead or dying hardwoods.

species.where: On soil or rotting wood under hardwoods and conifers.
features: Tough, yellow-brown, cracked, scaly skin
Very firm
Inside turns purple-black early, never pure white for long
species.lookalikes: True puffballs are soft and evenly white inside when young.
species.search: pigskin poison puffball (earthball) scleroderma citrinum on soil or rotting wood under hardwoods and conifers.

species.where: Lawns, roadsides, wood chips, and disturbed ground, often in groups.
features: Tall white cylindrical cap with shaggy upturned scales
Gills turn black and dissolve into ink from the bottom up
Loose ring on a hollow stem
species.lookalikes: Common ink cap (Coprinopsis atramentaria) is gray and smoother, and makes people sick when taken with alcohol.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.season_label: Apr, May, Jun, Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov
species.search: shaggy mane coprinus comatus lawns, roadsides, wood chips, and disturbed ground, often in groups.

species.where: In wood chips, mulch, and rich soil, often in gardens.
features: Starts as a white 'egg' half-buried in mulch
Hatches into a spongy stalk tipped with slimy, foul-smelling olive spores
Flies gather on it
species.lookalikes: The egg stage looks like a puffball or an Amanita button; cut it in half and you see jelly layers.
species.search: stinkhorns phallus ravenelii and mutinus elegans in wood chips, mulch, and rich soil, often in gardens.

species.where: Dense clusters on stumps and logs, hardwood and conifer.
features: Sulfur-yellow caps, darker orange centers
Gills yellow then greenish-gray; purple-brown spore print
Bitter taste
species.lookalikes: Honey mushroom has white gills and a white spore print.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.season_label: May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov
species.search: sulfur tuft hypholoma fasciculare dense clusters on stumps and logs, hardwood and conifer.

species.where: Overlapping shelves on dead hardwood logs, stumps, and branches.
features: Thin, leathery, fan-shaped caps in concentric bands of brown, gray, rust, and blue
Fuzzy upper surface
Tiny white pores underneath, 3 to 5 per millimeter
species.lookalikes: False turkey tail (Stereum ostrea) looks similar from above but has a smooth underside with no pores. Neither is dangerous; check the underside.
species.note: Old caps last all year. Fresh growth is most visible in late summer and fall.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.search: turkey tail trametes versicolor overlapping shelves on dead hardwood logs, stumps, and branches.

species.where: In clusters on dead hardwood, especially elm and willow, in cold weather and even winter thaws.
features: Sticky orange-brown cap
Dark brown, velvety stem base
White spore print
species.lookalikes: Deadly galerina grows in the same habitat and has a rusty brown spore print and a ring.

2009-11-19_Flammulina_sp_biolib.cz.jpg: František ŠARŽÍK
derivative work: Ak ccm

species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.season_label: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, Oct, Nov, Dec
species.search: velvet foot flammulina velutipes in clusters on dead hardwood, especially elm and willow, in cold weather and even winter thaws.

species.where: In wood chips, garden beds, and mulched paths.
features: Burgundy to tan cap
Gills gray then purple-black; dark purple-brown spore print
Thick, cogwheel-like ring on the stem
species.lookalikes: Other mulch mushrooms, including Agrocybe and Psilocybe, also have brown spore prints.

species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.season_label: May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct
species.search: wine cap stropharia rugosoannulata in wood chips, garden beds, and mulched paths.

species.where: On dead hardwood branches, often appearing after rain in cool weather.
features: Bright yellow to orange, wavy, brain-like jelly
Shrinks to a hard crust when dry and swells after rain
species.lookalikes: Orange jelly (Dacrymyces chrysospermus) is similar but grows on conifer wood.
species.note: It is actually a parasite of crust fungi on the wood.
species.regions_attr: northeast southeast midwest south-central rockies pacific-northwest california
species.search: witch's butter tremella mesenterica on dead hardwood branches, often appearing after rain in cool weather.

species.where: On dead hardwood or conifer branches and logs.
features: Brown, rubbery, ear-shaped
Translucent when held up to light
Smooth inner surface
species.lookalikes: Few look-alikes. Some cup fungi are brown but brittle, not rubbery.

species.search: wood ear auricularia americana group on dead hardwood or conifer branches and logs.
